newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-MALDINI WINS OVER PUBLIC BUT STRUGGLES TO WIN MATCH.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MALDINI WINS OVER PUBLIC BUT STRUGGLES TO WIN MATCH.

text.p: Cesare Maldini may have won over Italians with his debut on the national bench but his team will struggle to win matches on the evidence of Wednesday's 2-0 victory over Northern Ireland in an international friendly.

Goals from Gianfranco Zola and Alessandro Del Piero, who scored with a stunning last-minute free-kick, were enough to win Maldini a standing ovation from 38,000 Sicilians packed into "La Favorita" stadium.
The reception contrasted sharply with the boos reserved for Maldini's unpopular predecessor Arrigo Sacchi after his team were eliminated from Euro 96.
But it could not hide the fact that Maldini's side suffered from the same glaring deficiency as Sacchi's teams -- a failure to convert territorial advantage into goals.
"We must do better," admitted Italy's new manager afterwards. "We have real problems in the final 25 metres."

Italy's goal-scoring problems will have encouraged England manager Glenn Hoddle, watching from the stands as he prepares for next February's crucial World Cup qualifier against Maldini's side at Wembley.
Italian football president Luciano Nizzola, who appointed Maldini to take over from Sacchi last December, took heart from the warmth of the Palermo crowd.
"This was only a test," he said. "What's really important is how the national team has reconquered the nation's affection."
In a rare display of national unity, Sicilians crowded into Palermo's stadium to celebrate former under-21 manager Maldini's first appearance on the bench since he replaced Sacchi.
"Forza Italia, let's start again," read one banner, unfurled as Maldini led his team through their pre-match warm-up.
"The public were extremely generous," said Maldini, who shrewdly selected Palermo as the venue for his first match .
The national side joined in the nationalist spirit, swapping their usual blue shirts and white shorts for an all-new blue strip -- a colour which traditionally symbolises Italian soccer.
Although one banner proclaimed "Never again, Sacchi", Maldini fielded a team which, on paper, resembled the side eliminated in the first round of Euro 96.
On the pitch, however, Maldini, a pupil of former Italy manager Enzo Bearzot, took Italy back in time by fielding a five-man defence with Ciro Ferrara as sweeper and his son Paolo as a centre-back.
The new-look Italy took the lead with their first attack.
In the 10th minute, Pierluigi Casiraghi was tripped as he moved for Demetrio Albertini's cross but the referee waved play on as the ball fell to the unmarked Zola in the area.

The diminutive playmaker from English premier league Chelsea sidestepped advancing goalkeeper Tommy Wright before finding the net with a shot from an acute angle which Wright could only help on its way in.
The Italians came close to going two-up in the 16th minute when Angelo Di Livio's searching cross picked out Casiraghi but the Lazio striker's shot was parried by Wright.
The Irish goalkeeper was tested again from the resulting corner but somehow scrambled Di Livio's volley off the line after fumbling his first save.
But despite dominating the rest of the match, time and again the Italians saw neatly constructed moves break down on the edge of a crowded Northern Irish penalty area.

For their part, the visitors, who have never won on Italian soil, hardly looked capable of equalising although James Quinn forced a full-length save from goalkeeper Angelo Peruzzi with a volley in the 55th minute.
It took an inspired free-kick from second-half substitute Del Piero to give an air of respectability to the scoreline.
Minutes after squandering an easier chance, the Juventus number 10 curled the ball in at Wright's near post from the far side of the penalty area.
It was enough to win the Italians a standing ovation and a mini-pitch invasion but Maldini was not fooled. "It's clear that the England match will be another story altogether," he said.
